title: Pygmalion (Selected Scenes & The Transformation of Eliza Doolittle)
author: George Bernard Shaw
source: Pygmalion: A Romance in Five Acts (1913)
citation: Shaw, George Bernard. Pygmalion: A Romance in Five Acts. Constable and Co., 1913.

sections.heading: Act 1: Covent Garden and the Power of Phonetics

epigraph.quote: A woman who utters such depressing and disgusting sounds has no right to be anywhere—no right to live. Remember that you are a human being with a soul and the divine gift of articulate speech.

paragraphs: Under the portico of St. Paul's Church in London's Covent Garden on a rainy night, a crowd of citizens from different social classes take shelter. Among them is Eliza Doolittle, an unkempt flower girl speaking a harsh Cockney dialect, and Henry Higgins, an eccentric professor of phonetics who can pinpoint any Londoner's birthplace within two streets by their accent.

Higgins arrogantly wagers with his colleague Colonel Pickering that in six months, through phonetics and elocution training alone, he can transform this ragged flower girl into a woman who could pass as a duchess at an ambassador's garden party. For Higgins, Eliza is not an autonomous person with feelings; she is merely an experimental subject—a lump of raw clay to be sculpted according to his phonetic vanity.

sections.heading: Act 3: Mrs. Higgins's At-Home & The Small Talk Experiment

epigraph.quote: The difference between a lady and a flower girl is not how she behaves, but how she's treated.

paragraphs: Several months into her training, Higgins tests Eliza at his mother's fashionable drawing room. Beautifully dressed and speaking with pristine aristocratic pronunciation, Eliza is instructed to keep to two topics: the weather and everybody's health. However, beneath the polished vowels, Eliza's lively working-class slang bursts through: 'What call would a man with that strength in him have to die of influenza? They done the old woman in!'

While Higgins and Pickering treat Eliza's performance as an amusing scientific parlor trick, Mrs. Higgins perceives the underlying tragedy: 'You certainly are a pair of babies, playing with your live doll! Have you thought of what is to be done with her, what is to become of her, after the experiment?' Higgins and Pickering have made Eliza unfit to earn her living on the streets, but have given her no money or social status to live as a gentlewoman.

sections.heading: Act 5: Eliza Reclaims Her Soul and Independence

epigraph.quote: If I can't have kindness, I'll have independence.

paragraphs: After successfully fooling the entire aristocratic assembly at the Ambassador's Ball, Higgins and Pickering return home celebrating their triumph, completely ignoring Eliza's hard work and dedication. Enraged by Higgins's callous ingratitude, Eliza throws his slippers at him and walks out.

In their final confrontation in Act 5, Eliza confronts Higgins not as an inferior creation, but as his intellectual equal. She refuses to remain his domestic servant or emotional punching bag. She threatens to teach phonetics herself, using the very methods Higgins taught her. When Higgins protests that he created her, Eliza proudly declares that Colonel Pickering taught her self-respect by treating her like a lady from the start. Shaking off Higgins's control, Eliza walks away into freedom, having truly authored her own transformation.
